BEST JAZZ The Best Jazz on Bandcamp, August 2026 By Dave Sumner · September 01, 2026

I try to mix things up. The strength of the modern jazz scene is its diversity—all of the different takes on this classic music evolving with time and geography and lived experiences. What we view as being jazz has morphed from its classic sounds and become increasingly disparate, the bird flying further from the nest with each year. Faced with that, I attempt to highlight something from as many types of expression as I can—a little something for everyone. Where this preamble leads us is to my sincere apology to the straight-ahead fans. There’s not much of a classic sound—old-school or modern—in this month’s column. The music of August’s column is experimental, forward-looking, strange, mysterious, and clearly not occupied with the defining characteristics of any one genre. Anyways: my apologies. Let’s begin.

The music of Henry Threadgill’s Zooid ensemble is an exquisite deformity, as if to prove that beauty lies at the center of everything, no matter how it may seem at first blush. The latest from the jazz legend is a case in point. Melodically speaking, it’s the equivalent of watching someone sleep, fitfully twitching their way through a nightmare. Rhythmically, too, for that matter. Though unconventional—and certainly straining any attempt to genre-tag—the music merely asks you to take it as it is, at which point it becomes quite personable. Strange, yes; but personable. And I say this as someone who has been listening to—and happily grappling with—Threadgill’s music for nearly four decades. Threadgill has this talent for shifting gears, and suddenly everything sounds familiar, though in a very out way, as it does here with “Red Admiral Red Moon Rising.” August is an embarrassment of riches, as Threadgill has another recording out this month, a trio session with pianist Vijay Iyer, and drummer Dafnis Prieto.

In addition to being actual collaborators, Jakob Bro and Paul Motian were very much musically birds-of-a-feather, with their talent for commingling tranquility and chaos being just one similarity. Crafting melodies that cut to the heart is another. These are the two qualities that predominantly inform the latest from Bro, performing some original pieces and some from the departed collaborator. The guitarist—joined by saxophonists Chris Cheek and Jesper Zeuthen; pianist Craig Taborn; double bassists Larry Grenadier and Anders Christensen; and drummers Marcus Gilmore and Brian Blade—carried the live performance energy of a week-long residency at the Village Vanguard into the studio for this recording. I was torn between embedding the lovely Bro composition “Saturday” and the ensemble’s rendition of Motian’s “It Should’ve Happened a Long Time Ago;” both speak eloquently to the heart of the album.

In the album’s liner notes, Melissa Aldana states, “Standards are such a deep part of our language. Recording them felt less like stepping away from our voices and more like revealing another side of them.” This perspective becomes particularly evident on their rendition of Charles Mingus’s “Duke Ellington’s Sound of Love.” Equal impressions of “this is a Charles Mingus melody” and “this is being played by Melissa Aldana and Linda May Han Oh” strike a perfect balance between the heart of the music and the personality of the musicians tapping into it. Interspersed with a few improvisations, and ending with an Oh original, it’s all compositions by the legends of jazz, and sounding very much like the music of today.

A wonderful soul-jazz session offered up this month by pianist-keyboardist Zaccai Curtis. Afro-Caribbean influences like the warmest smile offered up in friendship. Curtis—joined by the core of tenor saxophonist Craig Handy, drummer Joe Dyson, and percussionist Brevan Hampden—gifts us music that perfectly complements the fading days of summer, when sunlight drenched afternoons are accompanied by the first hints of autumn carried on a gently cool breeze.

There’s a balance achieved on Parabólica, creating a surface of beauty so delicate that it sounds at risk any time this 20-piece ensemble threatens to harness its full strength. That tension is positively addictive. Sure, we’ll go with large ensemble, but there’s an orchestral behavior at play here, a sweeping grandeur that takes things harmonically to great heights. Conductor Gaia Wilmer’s latest embrace of influential composers focuses this time on the music of Gilberto Gil, so the Brazilian music influence is everywhere, but within that large ensemble-orchestral framework that just gives it an expansive feel, as if Wilmer were causing to emerge unexplored space in the original compositions. There’s some seriously breathtaking moments on this session.

The music of Ben Goldberg exists in two different eras. There’s no mistaking his very modern sound as being anything other than the sound of today—except possibly what he’ll decide tomorrow should look like. But there’s an old-school sensibility to the clarinetist’s music, the feeling that he’s tapped into the history of his instrument and jazz’s traditions even if he chooses, instead, to channel them through a different lens. In August, he released eight different recordings. Amassed over the last few years, they’re seeing the light of day for the first time. Different personnel, different formations (two duos, three trios, two quartets, and a quintet), different sounds and approaches. Note: Goldberg is offering up a free sampler for those needing a bit more of a nudge to listen in. I’ll also nudge you to give his 2013 release Unfold Ordinary Mind a listen, because I still find time to give it a listen after all these years.

A theme album where both the theme and its message remain a mystery. That lack of resolution is a big reason why outside will keep pulling listeners back into its orbit. Perhaps to figure things out, or just to relive the tension of encountering the unidentifiable. Keith Jafrate’s vision is one of the multi-genre spanning sessions that have become typical to this column, and a joy to this writer’s ears. The saxophonist—joined by pianist Laura Cole, violinist Faith Brackenbury, guitarist (and electronics specialist) Johnny Hunter, and bassist John Pope—alters textures between pieces, their interconnectedness only becoming obvious after the final note is achieved.

The music here summons the image of a shattered window pane fragmenting into a thousand pieces before smashing against the ground. It’s rhythmically fascinating, and any inclinations toward melody are merely glimpses reflected in the surface of all the moving pieces. The trio of pianist Kaja Draksler, bassist Petter Eldh, and drummer Christian Lillinger maintain a furious pace, or the impression of it during those times they give themselves away to the momentum they’d built up to that point.

I adore how Kjetil Møster adds the exclamation point to the end of his group’s go-by. It’s undeniably appropriate. The raw power exerted by this quartet of saxophonist Møster, electric guitarist Hans Magnus Ryan, electric bassist Nikolai Hængsle, and drummer Kenneth Kapstad is enough to make gasoline spontaneously ignite. The music is definitely fire. After the first time I saw Peter Brötzmann perform live—with a similar channeling of pure, raw intensity—I could never not shout his last name. Some just earn it. Møster! sure does. Fair warning: do not let your guard down just because they enter a melodic interlude or tease with an introspective passage.

There’s an ever-changing dynamic to Martin Küchen’s various Angles ensembles. When they bring larger numbers, as they often do, they buoy their outside-in approach with a wildly harmonic sound and a cutting melodicism. On this session, the saxophonist scales things down to a quartet, with previous Angles members Ingebrigt Håker Flaten (double bass), Mattias Ståhl (vibraphone), and Kjell Nordeson (drums), revisiting older compositions and taking advantage of the extra space the smaller formation provides.

I mean, this is just stunning: a duo session with Rodrigo Amado on tenor saxophone and David Maranha on electric organ. Light and shadow. Fire and water. Opposites, but united. One single piece, over 42 minutes in length, Maranha maintaining a wavering drone—a comforting sound but with an undercurrent of tension, too. Amado taking off in flight, but staying close to the ground, as if riding the air currents whipped up by the surface of Maranha’s organ. Staring into the flame can provoke a hypnotic reaction, of sensing things beyond the heat. This music, the same. It’s spiritual. Heart and soul.

Danny Keane’s Kinesis carves out a space where electronic music, European jazz, krautrock, and ambient cohabitate with minimalism, Indian classical, and modern jazz. It’s a heady concoction, teeming with activity. When the ensemble shifts into a straight-ahead modern sound on “A Major Minor Waltz,” the effect is almost jarring. Ruth Goller and Sarathy Korwar are two of the contributors familiar to readers of this column.

Other Albums of Note:

Joel Harrison’s octet (which includes three guitarists) got together at the 2025 Big Ears Festival for a performance of Miles Davis’s In a Silent Way. The song “Ngayaya” on the latest from vocalist Somi sidetracked me many times from listening to the music waiting impatiently in my August queue. The woozy melodicism on this trio session from pianist Leo Genovese, double bassist Takashi Sugawa, and drummer Alfred Vogel is highly personable, and a source of serious whimsy (released on Boomslang Records). The scattered marbles interactions between saxophonist Arman Sangalang and guitarist Dave Miller on this post-bop set is particularly appealing (released on Calligram Records). This straight-ahead session from pianist Daniel Vadillo attains a harmonic warmth and vibrancy by blending the music influences of his Mexico City roots with those of a more traditional modern jazz sound.
